title: One God: Monotheism
lead: The Bible's claim that the LORD alone is God grows from the first commandment, "You must not have any other gods in my presence" (Exodus 20:3), to Deuteronomy's "Apart from him there is no other" (Deuteronomy 4:35) and Isaiah's "I am the first and I am the last" (Isaiah 44:6). Scholars debate when Israel moved from worshiping one God among many to denying that other gods exist.

sections.h: From the first command to the New Testament
sections.b: The Ten Words forbid Israel to have other gods (Exodus 20:3), without saying whether they exist. Deuteronomy 4 goes further: the LORD is God "in the sky above and on the earth below. There is no other" (Deuteronomy 4:39), and the Shema confesses that the LORD is one (Deuteronomy 6:4). Elijah's contest on Mount Carmel asks the people to decide who is God (1 Kings 18:21–39). The prophets of the exile mock idols as wood and metal and declare that there is no God besides the LORD (Isaiah 44:6–20; Isaiah 45:5–22). Yet other texts speak of a council of heavenly beings around God (Psalm 82; Job 1:6). The New Testament keeps the confession of one God (Mark 12:29; 1 Corinthians 8:4–6; James 2:19) while confessing Jesus as Lord, which led to the later doctrine of the Trinity.
